title: The AI Lawyer
answer: Ten areas where artificial intelligence is changing legal work: discovery, contracts, research, corporate governance, intellectual property, litigation strategy, firm operations, privacy, the law being written now, and the security audits underneath all of it.

children.blurb: Predictive coding, cross-lingual review, audio and video evidence, privilege logging, and sentiment analysis of corporate messaging.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in legal work is not one system but a set of tools applied to specific tasks, from finding documents and drafting clauses to checking filings and auditing security. It is doing real work now in e-discovery, where machine learning ranks documents for relevance, and in contract review, where software flags risky clauses and standard terms. Legal research tools retrieve case law and suggest arguments, while compliance systems monitor regulatory changes and corporate governance teams track board obligations and filing deadlines. Intellectual property groups use it to search prior art and watch for trademark conflicts, litigation teams use analytics to estimate case timelines and judge behavior, and firm operations use AI for billing, matter management, and conflict checks. Privacy and security audits use AI to find data flows and access gaps, and the law being written now includes state bills and court rules that try to define when AI use must be disclosed. This section covers those ten areas as they operate, not as they are imagined.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven: e-discovery is the most mature, with courts accepting predictive coding for over a decade, but no system reliably understands meaning in ambiguous documents. Contract drafting tools handle standard clauses well but still miss novel risk allocation, and legal research is fast but can hallucinate case names, with accuracy problems documented. Litigation prediction remains descriptive, not prescriptive, because past outcomes do not determine future ones, and corporate compliance tools can flag deadlines but cannot interpret vague regulations. Intellectual property search is useful for exact matches but weak on conceptual similarity, and the site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows how much of the field is still being fought over rather than settled. There are 29 AI case law precedents, a small number that leaves many questions open. State AI bills number 6,895, but most are proposed, not enacted, and they conflict across jurisdictions, while security audits are improving but still rely on manual review for high-risk systems, and the honest limit is that AI reduces search and drafting time, and it does not replace legal judgment.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: E-Discovery and Large-Scale Document Analysis explains the most proven use of AI in law and sets the pattern for how machine learning handles evidence. Contract Lifecycle and Algorithmic Drafting then shows how the same ranking and extraction techniques move from past documents to future obligations. Legal Research and Case Strategy connects retrieval to argument, while Corporate Governance and Regulatory Compliance turns to the rules that firms must follow. Intellectual Property and Trademark Strategy covers the area with the most active disputes, given the 92 IP lawsuits tracked on this site, and Litigation Prediction and Judicial Analytics explains what can and cannot be inferred from court data. Legal Operations, Infrastructure and Security looks at the internal systems that make all of this possible, and Data Privacy and Cyber-Regulatory Compliance addresses the overlapping duties around personal data. Emerging Legal Frameworks collects the statutes and court rules still being written, and AI Security Audits and Enterprise Enablement closes the loop by describing how organizations test these tools before trusting them.
